title: Young stars at home in an ancient cluster
caption: The globular cluster NGC 6752, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 6752 · constellation Pavo · about 13000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Countless stars crowd this Hubble image of NGC 6752, a globular cluster, a dense ball of stars bound by gravity. At over 10 billion years old, it is one of the most ancient star clusters known, and has been shining for well over twice as long as our Solar System has existed.

The cluster is rich in blue stragglers, and some are visible here. These stars look younger than their neighbours, even though models suggest most stars in a globular cluster formed at about the same time. Where they come from is something of a mystery.

NGC 6752 may help explain them. A very high share of the stars in its core, up to 38%, appear to be binary systems, pairs of stars orbiting each other. In such a crowded, turbulent region, collisions between stars could produce the many blue stragglers seen there.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.12 x 1.48 arcminutes) and distance (13000 light years), the frame spans roughly 8 × 5.6 light-years. Its light set out about 13,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using filters at 555, 606 and 814 nm, in visible and near-infrared light. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble separates individual stars that would blur together through a small telescope.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: NGC 6752 lies 13 000 light-years away in the constellation of Pavo, far beyond our reach, yet the clarity of Hubble's images brings it, and its puzzling blue stragglers, tantalisingly close for astronomers to study.
alt: A dense field of countless stars forming a globular cluster.
